utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The SDS used weapons confiscated from the Territorial Defence, and as I said before, weapons that were also from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have information about certain people who did that in certain areas of the Srebrenica and Bratunac municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In early 1992, it was not a secret. We had operative information, and we knew exactly who was doing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, according to your information, who was in charge of arming Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Zekic was mostly in charge of arming the town of Srebrenica, and Miodrag Jokic, called Miro, for the area of Studenac. Yes. Allow me to finish, please. For the Studenac area Zoran Spajic and Rado Simic. For the area or the village of Sijemovo, Milan Zekic, Maksim Zekic, called Makso. For the area or the village of Dubova. The Ilic and Obranavic brothers. For the area of Vijogor, which is part of Orahovica, Milos Milovanovic, Dusan Vasic. For the area of Fakovici and Ratkovici, and here I would like to note that the Fakovici and Ratkovici area a person, an employee of the elementary school in Fakovici, Slavko Jovanovic. And Stanisa and Milenko Stevanovic were also associates in the area of Ratkovici. For the area of Sase with hamlets, it was Sreten Ilic, Momcilo Cvetinovic, Bato Rankic. That was up to the Bjelovac part of the region. For the Skelani local commune area Dusko Mandic, former police employee who was fired because of some criminal activities earlier relating to that. Dusko Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the Sase area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Sase area was covered by Stjepan Novakovic, called Krke, and I already mentioned Bato Rankic. I apologise. I said Bato Rankic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the usher now show the witness document Bosnian Muslim the commander of the battalion. MR. DI FAZIO: Just in order to understand the evidence, the witness described people being responsible for arming of Serbs in the area, in these various areas, and two of them were Stanisa and Milenko Stevanovic who were also associates in the area of Ratkovici. I don't know if the witness means they were associates, friends, or whether they were associate armers of the population. I'll just not sure what that means. I wonder if that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic, you were obviously listening or hearing -- hearing what the witness himself said. Is this a question of interpretation or perhaps you can address the witness directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously unclear interpretation. The witness said Slavko Jovanovic with his associates Stanisa and Milenko Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we will come back more specifically to this question. Witness, could you please look at a document by the battalion command from Fakovici dated 3rd of April, 1993, with the number 04360175. And now I'm going to read this document. It's brief. "Certificate confirming that Milosevic Vesko was assigned an Schmiesser last year in the unit in Fakovici at the time. From that time period until today, the above-named person assisted with all possible transport and work relating to war activities. "For his personal safety on water and in a boat, he was assigned the above-mentioned weapon which was registered in the book of assigned weapons. Field commander at the time, Slavko Jovanovic from Fakovici distributed the weapons. We are not in possession of the book of assigned weapons because it was with Slavko. Since he was killed, we do not know where the book is." I would now like you -- to ask you the following: Slavko Jovanovic, who according to this document was the field commander at the time in Fakovici, is that the person about whom you in the Srebrenica police had information that he was arming Serbs in the Fakovici area even before the war began?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, do you see in this document where it says: "From that time period until today, the above-named person assisted with all possible transport and work for the war activities, and for his personal safety on water and in a boat he was assigned the above-mentioned weapon." I would like to draw your attention to the date, the 3rd of April, 1993. Do you agree that this certificate talks about the year before, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that the document states that Slavko Jovanovic died?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that he died? And if you did, when did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what period?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: In the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the police before the war, did you have information that weapons were being transported from Serbia to the Fakovici area or not?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The Fakovici area was one of the key weapons distribution points from Serbia in this area and broader than Ratkovici. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For this document which consists of two pages, one in Serbo-Croat and the other one in English with ERN 04360175 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D844.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Ratkovici in connection with arms distribution. Do you remember any special points or incidents connected with this?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a police officer, an official of the police station, after the 20th of March, 1992, we received information that in the village of Ducici, in the Ratkovici area, a military helicopter had landed and that weapons had been brought in. Also, that General -- other, rather, a major of the former JNA, Milenko Jovanovic had arrived by helicopter personally and that he was distributing weapons there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself go to the spot in Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was on duty that day, and this was terrain that I personally was responsible for along with Mr. Hasan Hajdarevic. I went out onto the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far did you manage to get?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: We got to a place between the village of Poznanovici and Ducici in the direction of Ducici where the villages of the Ratkovici local commune begin, and between Poznanovici and Ducici we were met by several Serbs who prevented us from entering Ducici and Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: They told us that we had no right to enter Serb villages, that this was Serbian business and that this was the job of the Serbian police, which they already had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you recognised anyone among the men who stopped you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was surprised, and I recognised Mr. Jovanovic, who was wearing a Serbian cap with a cockade. Also, Stanisa and his relative Milenko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to Stanisa Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Stanisa Stevanovic and his relative Milenko Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they behave towards you two police officers? But before that, let me ask you, did you know these people from before? For example, Stanisa Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew them all personally, because this was the area I was responsible for as a police officer, and I knew every man on the ground relatively well. I knew Mr. Stanisa Stevanovic very well in the line of duty, because he had a criminal record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what this was about?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: He had committed -- MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, please. If Your Honours please, I'm standing up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish. Let him finish first, please. Then I think I anticipate what you're going to say. Yes. Finish answering the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This was a person who was prone to disturbing public law and order, quarrels, fights, and there was one crime of murder, illegal wood cutting and exploitation of timber, frequent conflicts with his neighbours, and also with his family in relation to property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: The evidence of the -- the murder, I think, was led in private -- private session. I don't think the evidence of the other offences was. From -- I'm talking from memory now, but I recall that he did give his evidence in private session. I think Mr. Jones was cross-examining him, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, too, and I remember also the information on disputes of land and on property and the rest of it. MR. DI FAZIO: That was about one specific crime. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I frankly don't see any problem in moving ahead and retaining the evidence as it is in public session for the time being, unless there is agreement on the part of the Defence on this, but it doesn't make a difference according to me if the other witness gave more details on this particular incident in private session. Now, the witness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. now isn't going into details here. He is just -- MR. DI FAZIO: Very well, Your Honour. I just remind -- remind of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is any concern also on the part of the Defence, then obviously we'll redact that part and deal with what comes out in private session. I have no problems with that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, we are not concerned about this. On the contrary. We feel that this testimony should be public. It has to do with the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you was: How did these people behave toward you two policemen on that occasion? And I am now referring to the Stevanovic cousins.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a very ugly situation. They practically chased us away in spite of our attempts to clarify that we had come with good intentions. They told us that they didn't need any Muslim police, that this was a matter for the Serbian police. They were very aggressive towards us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you learn exactly what happened there in spite of this?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The information we had received previously was confirmed by citizens who were Muslim inhabitants of Poznanovici and later on honourable Serbs from the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any events having to do with the reserve police force in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Things were very complex as regards the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any incidents in connection with the reserve police from Skelani?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Srebrenica, in late January or early February, our operative information in the Srebrenica police station was that weapons were being distributed in the town of Srebrenica opposite the Baratova petrol pump. So I personally went there with my colleagues, and there we confiscated two semi-automatic rifles from employees of the then company called Faros from a Skoda car, which was white, and its licence plate was 11009 with the letters ZV in front of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with rifles after that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: We put the rifles in the police station in Srebrenica and soon afterwards the Srebrenica police station was surrounded by a large number, several hundred citizens of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone enter the police station to intervene?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Serb citizens, their representative and leader, the leader of the SDS, Goran Zekic, entered the police station. With him was Miodrag Jokic, also known as Miro, in a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they looking for in the police station? Why had they come?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: They wanted the confiscated weapons, those two semi-automatic rifles, to be returned and issued to -- to Serbs from Skelani who were reservists, and they insisted on two brothers, the Gligic brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you before that. Were the Gligic brothers reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: On that same day, they were quickly received into the reserve police force and issued with those two weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of them from before?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of them used to play football in the Bubar football team, in team number 1. His name was Branko. We used to call him Brano. And they had a nickname, Pira [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall some events in early April 1992 connected with the immediate vicinity of Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember something to do with the village of Poljanci?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that day I set out from my own village, Susnjari, to go to Slatina, and in the village of Poljanci, at the crossroads, I was stopped by six armed Serbs from Lipenovici, Jezestica, and their leader, as far as I could see was Ljuban Blagovcanin [phoen] who had with him a German Schmeisser. Two of those present had two automatic rifles, two had semi-automatic rifles, and the sixth man who was some 30 or 40 metres away had a light machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Poljanci part of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That territory is physically connected to Jezestica through Buljim and Lipenovici. It's physically connected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These men, were they wearing uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: They were in olive-drab uniforms of the former Territorial Defence or the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information about what was happening in the area of Skelani in March and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Skelani we had a police department. It was part of the Srebrenica police department, and at that time the Serb municipality of Skelani was formed as was the Serb police station of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the usher now please show the witness Defence Exhibit D603. This is a decision on the establishment of the Skelani Serb municipality, and the date is the 22nd of March, 1992. I will quote to you.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. I can't read very well even with glasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will quote this part. Take a look, please. Could you just follow what I'm reading. It says: "A Skelani municipality Serbian Assembly shall be set up with its seat in Skelani. "The newly founded Serbian municipality of Skelani covers part of the territory belonging to the former municipalities of Srebrenica and Bratunac with a predominantly Serbian population. From Srebrenica municipality, the following cadastral districts: Skelani, Kalimanici, Zabokvica, Gaj, Pribidoli, Toplica, Medje, Radosevici, Brezani, Ratkovici, Opravdici, Postolja, Krnici, Blazjevici, Godjevici, Bozici, Pribojevici, Kostolomci, Bujakovici, Crvica, Petrica and Isakovici. "From Bratunac municipality, the following cadastral districts: Zlijebac, Jaketici, Vrankovi, Boljevici, Fakovici, Stanatovici, Mlecva, Vranesevici, Loznica, Tegare, Sikirici, and Bjelovac." In connection with this, I will ask you the following: In April 1992, did you have information to the effect that this newly established Skelani Serbian municipality was taking parts of Srebrenica and Bratunac municipalities, including Ratkovici, Fakovici, Bjelovac and Sikirici?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now please try to remember what was happening at that time. You can put that document back. In early April 1992 in the police station or administration of Srebrenica, what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: At Srebrenica police station at the time, certain Serb police officers were leaving the Srebrenica police station. Some were going to the Srebrenica police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment. I apologise, but you said that Serb police officers were separating. Some of them were leaving. Can you please tell us where they were doing?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: To the newly formed police station in Skelani and to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember a joint meeting with the Serbs relating to the falling apart of the police station if this did occur?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well. I remember it very well. I will never forget it. It was a very heavy kind of meeting. It took place between the 12th and the 13th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you the following: Do you remember whether all of the Serb police officers reacted in the same way to this falling apart of police station?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were those who were in favour of continuing work together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything specific in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that meeting, Milun Perendic stood up, started to cry and said, "You Muslims manage however you can. A great evil is awaiting you. Don't think that I am telling you this as a Serb, but I am saying it as a man, and what I am telling you will have major consequences for me, and it's a question of how am I going to reach Bajina Basta." That's the place where his family was and where he had his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if any of the local Serbs supported him in what he said?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a few did, but what stuck in my mind specifically was when Borivoje Marinkovic stood up and also started to cry and practically repeated the same words. And then he said that for the last month, since early March, something like that, his family was exposed to major pressure. He was living above the police station in the same building. He said that they were being exposed to pressure, that there was tapping, wire-tapping. People were listening to what was happening at the police station, and they were asking them for information, for data about what was actually going on at the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, and what was the reaction of the other Serb police officers other than those two?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Borivoje Marinkovic didn't even finish what he was saying. The other police officers present, Serb police officers, led by Milisav Gavric, Dusko Neskovic, and then inspector Milisav Ilic literally jumped up from their places, attacked Mr. Perendic, and Mr. Marinkovic. They said that they were traitors of the Serbian people and that they were favouring the Muslims. And they also used the term "balija" for us in later discussions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did this meeting end?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Not very well. When we came outside again there were several hundred people in groups around the police station. These were Serb citizens, and it seemed, at least to me, as if everything was organised and planned. So it was -- we just barely made it out of that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us whether you continued to go to work over the following few days?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, just let me finish. I apologise to the Trial Chamber. We left the police station thanks to the fact that Gavric Milisav said to the present Serb citizens, "It's all very well. You can all go home now. Everything is going to be fine in the next few days," and then we continued with our normal work at the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, the Muslim police officers, did you understand that a war was being prepared?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. It was all clear to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to organise yourselves in order to get weapons and some other means?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to organise ourselves to get some weapons and materiel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you manage to get anything?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. With a number of prominent Muslims, we managed to collect a few automatic rifles, also radio communication devices, as many as we could get.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you put the things that you managed to get?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Hamed Salihovic was the chief of the police station. We gave these things to him and he took those things to his own apartment. It was a studio apartment in Srebrenica and he also put that in his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out what happened with the weapons and equipment and the radio communication devices?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: When one delegation, one political delegation from Srebrenica, which also included Mr. Hamed Salihovic was there on the 17th of April in 1992 -- actually, they went to the Fontana restaurant in Bratunac for negotiations, somebody, an unidentified person -- or a number of unidentified persons broke into Mr. Hamed Salihovic's apartment and his office, took all the things that were collected. They even took away his personal documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was happening at the same time with the civilian Serb population, let's say from the Kravica area, including Jezestica and broader in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: In April and even earlier in the Kravica area, and not only the area of Kravica but the areas of other Serb villages, women and children began to leave more and more often to Ljubovija and other areas. Let me say here that only men who were fit for military service stayed behind, as well as women who agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have information about what was going on in mid-April in Bratunac and its environs, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was happening? Did somebody arrive there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th of April, 1991 -- 1991, at about 1300 hours, units came from the Vukovar front. These were Arkan's men, Seselj's men, and always some members of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, are you talking about the 17th of April, 1991, or 1992 when you're talking about the arrival of these troops to -- these units to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 17th of April, 1992 or the 17th of April, 1991, when you're talking about the arrival of Arkan's and Seselj's men to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you personally a participant in a political event in that period around the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what happened?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, 1992, on the 17th of April, a political delegation from Srebrenica completed a meeting around 1500 hours which we did not know about in Bratunac. These were negotiations which I said were also attended by Mr. Hamed Salihovic. After that, at approximately 2200 hours in the evening on the 17th of April, 1992, we received an ultimatum or a last call from the Bratunac police station that someone representing the police should come for talks or negotiations to Bratunac, to the Fontana because the representatives of the political authorities or the civilian authorities did not turn up. We actually didn't know anything about that meet going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to Bratunac? Who went to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I have to mention at that time and to this very day am friends with many of those Serbs. It was decided that I should go and Mr. Alija Hasic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who you talked with over there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: On our way into the restaurant, the Fontana restaurant we were greeted by Mirodrag Jokic, Miro, Sreten Radic, Bjelevoj Ostorak [phoen], and the following persons did not talk to us. They just were issuing orders about what we should do. Deronjic. A representative of the military. His last name was Reljic. I don't know his first name. A representative of Arkan's men was also there, of Seselj's men, too, and they were wearing different camouflage uniforms which were quite new to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they asking you to do?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: They were stating an ultimatum that all the Muslims had to hand in their weapons by 8.00 a.m. in Dugo Polje at Zuti Most at the house of Mevdo Avdagic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: We tried to convince them that this was physically impossible and that we should try to reach some kind of acceptance on their part to extend this deadline a little bit, because some places in the Srebrenica and Bratunac area were even 40 kilometres apart, 40 or 30 kilometres from this location where we were supposed to hand in the weapons or where the citizens were supposed to hand in the weapons. So it was practically impossible to carry out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like the usher to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit P90, and it's page 41 in Bosnian, and it has the number 02919258, and that is actually page 21 in English, and it has the number 00186691. I would like to quote just a small excerpt from the book which describes this event. It's a book by Naser Oric called "Srebrenica." On page 41, Witness, on the bottom I am going to quote: "During the day in Bratunac there was a delegation from Srebrenica which came on its own initiative represented by police officers, Sidik Ademovic and Jusuf Hasic, who requested that the deadline be extended as much as possible in order to gain time. The Serbs did extend the deadline but for two hours only: Until 10 a.m. on 18 April 1992. They managed to extend the time for two more days." Please, who was it who went with you to Bratunac? Was it Jusuf Hasic or Alija Hasic?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, gentlemen, the information that is correct here is only Sidik Ademovic. That is the only correct information, that I was present. Jusuf Hasic was not, and we did not seek, but I repeat we received instructions in the form of an ultimatum how and in which manner to behave. It was an ultimatum issued by the Serb representatives, I repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it described correctly here that you managed to extent the deadline?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just allow me to ask you. Besides Alija Hasic who you said went with you, is there also a Jusuf Hasic in your area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Jusuf Hasic is a person who was in his 60s at that time. He was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an employee of Domavija [phoen]. It's a rehabilitation centre belonging to the Gubur Spa in Srebrenica and he was the uncle of Alija Hasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Alija Hasic was with you at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then is this part of the book correct? Does it reflect what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. After this, did you return to the Srebrenica police station that day?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we returned. Actually, I returned to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to Srebrenica it was the first time that I was captured by the Serbs. I already saw Serbs who had captured the police station. I saw Mr. Zlatko there. The post of chief was taken over by Radisa, an employee of a zinc factory in Potocari and his neighbour Bakrija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Zlatan's last name?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. I can't remember it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And what happened from that time on?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: From that time on, my trip --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anyone intervene so that they would release you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The only way out for me then was to contact the Bratunac police station. I was in touch with Luka Bogdanovic, and he issued an order to the gentlemen in question to release me so that I could go to him in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to Bratunac? What happened?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I saw and understood what was actually going on, and I went through the woods and over the hills to my Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, what happened from late April to early May 1992? What was going on in that area? You said that you went to Susnjari. Well, let's make it a little shorter. Did refugees start arriving to the Susnjari area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In April and May and the period which followed after that, countless refugees arrived from all directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Susnjari, my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell Their Honours where these refugees came from.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: From all directions, but mostly from Bratunac, Glogova, Koloma [phoen], Zelena, along the Drina from Bratunac towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did these people tell you what had happened to them and why they were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They recounted horrifying stories of what they had been through and what they had seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, for example, an event recounted to you by people from Lonjin? Can you first show Their Honours where Lonjin is?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you spoke to someone from Lonjin and what they told you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with several refugees, but there was one lady in particular, her name was Sabina, who told me something that touched me, something that I will never forget. She said to me that in that area children and elderly people had been slaughtered, between 30 and 40 of them, that there had been arrests of women and children, that girls were raped and slaughtered. And she told me about a neighbour of hers, Sadika. The local Serbs caught her, raped her, impaled her and then threw her into the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you what happened to this lady's children? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Sadika's children were among the group in which Madam Sabina was, and they watched this from the woods nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these children alive today? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the children survived, and they are in a European country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. These people you spoke to, did they tell you who the organisers and executioners of these crimes were?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not individually but collectively. Everybody said that it was the local police, representatives of the Territorial Defence, SDS members, and volunteers, that is, foreigners from the Republic of Serbia, but most of all it was their neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may the witness be shown Defence Exhibit D430. This is a document issued by the Birac Brigade. The 1st battalion command, Osmaci, of the 1st of February, 1993. The number is 01283527, and it is signed by Commander Bosko Djuricic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will quote the document to you. It says here: "In May 1992, we lent a TAM-150 motor vehicle owned by the Yugoslav army, a unit that was stationed in Osmaci, and a Puch jeep motor vehicle owned by Petar Jankovic from Kalesija to a volunteer unit under the command of the so-called Simo Chetnik. "After this unit was taken out of the Birac Brigade and integrated in the Zvornik Brigade, these vehicles were not taken from it because the unit because the unit fought in the area of the Birac and the Drina Corps." My question in connection with this is: Have you ever heard of this volunteer unit of the so-called Simo Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The refugees who arrived from the area of Zelena, Drinjaca, Zvornik, Kamenica, and Kula, they very often mentioned this gentleman called Simo Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours exactly when the refugees came to Susnjari from these areas?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: They arrived in June, July, and right until the fall of Cerska and Pobrdje, and they were all in Srebrenica municipality, what was left of the free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these refugees which you said arrived in the areas of Susnjari and the Zvornik villages, did they speak about the relations between the Serb volunteers and the local Serb units?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: It was the same as that of the local population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was: Did you know whether these units acted together with the local Serbs or not?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the atrocities you described, did you receive similar information from refugees arriving from other areas? You mentioned a little while ago that refugees from Suha and Borkovac had came to your village.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They spoke of horrifying situations, arrests, executions, massacres in the area of the village of Suha and Borkovac, which is contiguous to Hranca in the direction of Glogova. And later on this was confirmed when mass graves were opened up and women and children were found inside. I think Their Honours are aware of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what they said? For example, how many people were killed in one spot in Borkovci?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: About 35.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Suha?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: 40, 42 maybe more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point did refugees arrive from Vlasenica in your village?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that period of time, there is no area in Bratunac and Vlasenica from which refugees did not arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember some refugees from the village of Pomol?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Not only Pomol but also Djile, Pomol, parts of Vlasenica. And a group which arrived from Pomol sticks in my memory because there was an old woman who had arrived with her daughter, and she asked me to hear her story and to help her if I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what had happened to her?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: She told me that in her village, Pomol, the population had been expelled, driven out into the woods, and one day she and her daughter returned to their house in order to prepare some food and to bake some bread. While she and her daughter were in the house, seven Serb men came in. They were armed. They raped her daughter while she watched. I will never forget that scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Her daughter, who at that time was 17 or 18, was all cut up as if she had been attacked by wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many houses were there in Susnjari more or less, and where did you put up all these refugees? How many refugees were there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: In my village of Susnjari there were about 40 houses, and as many refugees as possible were accommodated in houses, but there were about one and a half thousand refugees, and they lived in the tables, under trees, in the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect did this have on the local population of Susnjari? Did they know of all the stories that you knew about?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They heard all this, saw it, and experienced it. Their blood froze. There was fear everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally have weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I had my hunting rifle, my official pistol. I had my official automatic rifle and a small Motorola which I took from the police station when I left the police station on the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from you, how many other people in Susnjari had weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: We had about 20 pieces of weaponry including licensed weapons, my own weapons, and this included pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss the situation with the local population, and did they consider the situation and reach some kind of decision? I'm referring to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was discussion about how we should either surrender or fight, and the decision that was reached was to fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a local group formed and was a leader elected?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After long discussions, they decided that I should be their leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the summer of 1992 until the end of 1992, did people join your group on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they entered the group, did they stay for a certain period of time? Tell Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was all voluntary, and no one was able to tell anyone else that they had to do something. The situation was disastrous as regards food and hunger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people simply leave and go off to other areas, people from your group?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From my group and also my neighbours and fellow villagers because there was shelling, there was hunger, there was fear, there was poverty, lack of accommodation. People were beginning to get sick and die.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people join your group who came from other areas?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to talk to the people who joined your group to convince them to stay and not to leave the group?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did everything to get them to stay, but there was nothing I could do for several reasons. There was hunger. There was fear. There was daily shelling. People were killed. There were attacks. The number of refugees increased day by day. The situation was really disastrous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area of Susnjari, was it in a particularly bad situation for some reason? Can you explain that to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the 2nd of May onwards, my village, Susnjari, was definitely physically cut off from every other Muslim village, and another peculiarity was that in terms of geographical elevation, it was the highest place and a third factor was that on the west, to the west side, it was physically connected to many Serb villages on the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show Their Honours this on the map? Please indicate the situation of your village and its relation to the villages from Jezestica, Kravica and Kajici and one side.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us exactly what you are indicating now. What is this line?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the line of physical separation of Susnjari from the rest of the Potocari local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the first village is from the top that you listened up with the line. Go in order.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Bukova Glava, Dubova, then Brosevici was cleansed at the time, linked up with Sijemovo, Orahovica, Vijogor and then the corridor continues to the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's from that side. What about the Jezestica area and from the other sides? Can you also draw the line? Could you indicate that for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have joined up are Serb villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned several times that Susnjari was shelled every day. Could you please tell us where, from which places was the shelling coming from.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: From Jezestica, Kravica, Siljkovici, Veresinje, Lipenovici, Rogac plateau, which was corps plateau. It was used by the Serb side. The area, the broader area of Kravica, the location of Brezik, and then a broader, larger plateau which was suitable for many military activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us where Brezik is?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: It's the area between Agici and Opravdici. I already circled it, but perhaps this area can be expanded. It's a larger plateau, a larger area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it could be used for different military purposes. Was this related to the artillery or something else?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: To the artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know you were shelled from these locations that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: My village, Susnjari, and Jaglici are the most elevated points in that area and I could see the entire area to the north towards Jezestica and Kravica. What I wasn't sure about, what I couldn't see I used my binoculars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides this group of yours which you said was armed and which you led in the Susnjari area, were there any other armed groups within this circle that you drew? Were there people in Jaglici, Brezova Njiva?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were about 15 of them and ten in Brezova Njiva. In Babuljice there were about 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these groups, did they act jointly with your group?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were independent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe your relationship to these groups? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: It was all independent. Nobody trusted anyone else. Everyone guarded their own village, their own house. It was such a situation that nobody knew whether they would see the night alive or see the morning alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who headed these various groups?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Alispahic Mujo headed the group in Jaglici. Zukic Velaga was at the head of the group in Brezova Njiva. Smailovic Meho was together with Mujo in Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Babuljice?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Babuljice, it was Mensur Mesanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you something else. In June -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please. I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem? MR. DI FAZIO: There is no substantial problem, Your Honours. I just wonder if we could get the spelling of those last names in the answer that came at lines 6, 7 and 8. It won't turn up in the transcript tonight and you can't study and look at documents unless you understand the correct spelling of the names. Madam Vidovic, I'm sure, would have the spelling of the names. You see, when this is printed out, there is just going to be squiggles tonight, and I can't understand and read this evidence overnight and this is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can quite understand and agree with you. The first one was Alispahic. MR. DI FAZIO: But it's the remainder really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The remainder we did go through them one by one. Do you need the first one to be spelled out? I think you -- MR. DI FAZIO: Probably safest, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the first one, Mr. Ademovic, was Alispahic Mujo, headed the group of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where -- where did he head the group? Maglyci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And his name is Alija Spahic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alispahic. That's a last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can someone spell it out for us? It's A-l-i for sure, Ali, and S-p-a-h-i-c, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next one, the next person you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I can do that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It will be quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be definitely quicker, Madam Vidovic, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please follow what I'm saying, Witness. Then you mentioned Velaga Zukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Brezova Njiva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: V-e-l-a-g-a, Z-u-k-i-c. Then you mentioned Mensur Mesanovic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: M-e-n-s-a-n-o-v-i-c, M-e-n-s-u-r. Mensur Mesanovic in Babuljice?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and in Jaglici. Besides Mujo Alispahic, there should also be the name of Meho Smailovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, S-m-a-i-l-o-v-i-c, M-e-h-o in Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I hope it's all clear now. THE PROSECUTOR: I'm very grateful to the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser was a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just before we continue now, the witness mentioned, said it was all independent. Nobody trusted anyone else. What is meant by not trusting anyone else? Was it distrust with regard to Serbs or distrust also between Muslim villages or leaders of Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm looking at the face of the witness, he's either not understood your question or the cause may be some kind of interpretation -- misinterpretation of what he may have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to repeat. It's at line 73, 1. It was all independent. Nobody trusted anyone else. Everyone guarded their own village. Now, you are speaking of -- that there was distrust between certain groups, and my question was: Between which groups was there some sort of distrust? Was it distrust from Muslims versus Serbian villages or was there also some distrust between Muslim villages or leaders of Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the trust between Serbs and Muslims -- or distrust between Serbs and Muslims existed from before, but there was also distrust between the group leaders, because everyone believed that they would be the ones to best protect and preserve their own village and their own citizens, the inhabitants of their own village. That was the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that clear enough for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June and July 1992, how many civilians were there in Susnjari, and -- and if you remember, how many refugees passed through Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: There were constantly about 1.500 in Susnjari. In June and July, I know that over 4.000 refugees passed through my area in Susnjari. Susnjari and Jaglici and Brezova Njiva, the ones that I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell the Trial Chamber where these refugees were passing and where were they going to?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The majority of these refugees tried and did end up going through Buljim, Djermani, Jezestica between Siljkovici and Mranice towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, in order to reach Konjevic Polje, the refugees had to pass very close to Serbian lines at Djermani and Jezestica. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Djermani and Jezestica. More precisely at Hajducko Groblje. This distance it was only 200 metres. The passage was just 200 metres broad between the two lines, and it was 1.5 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show the Trial Chamber the area where Ravna Gora and Ravni Boljum are?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is that area. Where did the refugees have to pass in order to reach Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: You see these two villages circled in red, Siljkovici on the right and Brezanci. Jaglici, Lupoglav. I'm going to mark that in green. I'm going to mark the direction they were going in green.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And could the refugees go to the other side, towards Potocari, or was your region of Susnjari, Jaglici and Brezova Njiva cut off in June and July from Bljecova, Pale, Milatcovici?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Like I said, on the 2nd of May my area was physically separate from everywhere else. The only open part was towards Slatina. It was a wooded area towards Suceska and Milici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the reason why the refugees used the road that you indicated?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the only way in and out. It was the only road that you could take. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier you mentioned that at least 4.000 refugees passed through Susnjari. They didn't stay long in Susnjari. Do you know anything about the fate of those people? What happened to the people who passed through this corridor?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The people who passed through the corridor either died or were wounded or massacred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? What was happening? How did they get killed?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Because they encountered ambushes, everyday minefields. They were exposed to shelling and all other kinds of means available to destroy a human being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to tell the people not to go, that they were going to their death?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in every possible way knowing what that area was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember events or an event in late July 1992 that relates to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened on the 29th of June? Was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In -- on the 29th of June in 1992, it's a date that I remember. A group consisting of over 800 people set out through the wilderness, through the woods, to Konjevic Polje. When they arrived at the Ravna Gora plateau, the Hajducko Groblje location, the Hajducko cemetery, they ran into an ambush, and most of them were either killed or seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to come to their assistance?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to help them or were all those people already dead? I didn't understand you properly.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those who had been killed had been killed, but 15 or 20 of us managed to get there, and we had a shoot-out with the Serbs, the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the usher now show the witness document D32. This is a record sheet for a dead combatant. Please look at this document which is dated the 29th of September, 1993. However, look at the contents of the document. It says first and last name, Mihajlo, son of Uros Uzelac, volunteer. Date and place of birth, Zemun. Is that in Serbia? Is Zemun in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Excuse me, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Days and place of death, 29th of June, Jezestica. How death occurred: In combat. Then look down here. Circumstances of death, it says "The above-named died in combat." He was killed in combat. You have now described the events of the 29th of June, 1992. Do you -- well, you said that you fought with the Serbs in order to help those civilians. First of all, you said a group of 800 civilians. How many civilians, Muslims, were killed on that spot? Can you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to give estimates. I know of 35 who were killed, 45 who were wounded either seriously or slightly. This is not an estimate. This is something I saw for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you tried to come to their aid. Were there any Serbs killed? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And some men from my group were also killed. We saw them dragging along the corpses of dead Serbs, because when we had this shoot-out with them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that civilians were passing close to the Serb lines. In June and July 1992, did you know what the disposition of the Serb lines was in your area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the usher now show the witness D35. This is an excerpt from a book entitled "The Bloody Christmas in the Village of Kravica." It's Boro Miljanovic. And I will quote the last paragraph on page 42 where it says: "In mid-April a Crisis Staff was formed, consisting of the following appointed persons: Nedjo Nikolic - chairman, Krsto Cvjetinovic, Radomir Raso Milosevic, Bogoljub Eric, Jovan Nikolic, known as Jole, Mile Milanovic, Dragan Ilic, Luka Bogdanovic, Slavisa Eric, and Nedeljko Nikolic. For safety reasons, the staff dismissed regular classes, and turned the school building into a barracks. Territorial formations were organised. "The staff determined defence lines in all settlements from Banjevici, Donja and Gornja Brana, Bacici, Jezero, Mratinjaci, Gornji and Donji Dolovi, Brezanci, Jasikovaca,, Ravni Boljum, Jezestica, (Jalgic, Djermani, Veresinje), via Avdanina Njiva and Mandici to Bandijera." Witness, does this document reflect reliably the disposition of the front lines in your area? Tell Their Honours which line you knew about from among these mentioned here and indicate it on the map.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: All these lines were known to me, but what I had a direct connection with was Siljkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you draw a line where you know there was a line, which is mentioned in this document? Only the ones you know about. Can you please link up these places by a line?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I have already done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So this is part of what you've already done. Can you indicate this Jezestica area and the line towards Jaglici, Djermani, Versenije? Have you done that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to be brief, does this document reliably describe the front line on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn of the existence of this line? I'm not speaking of before the war but of June and July 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Every day people went to observe certain areas. I'm referring now to Djermani, Jezestica, Siljkovici, Lipanovic, Brezanci, and Poljanci. Every day they went to observe and reconnoiter and, we received information, and if something was not clear to me, as I knew the area well, I had been born there, I was a hunter, and I had privately in my personal life lived with these people, I went on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says in the record we received information. Let's clarify this. From whom did you personally receive information?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: From my men in the group who went to observe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, to finish with this document, I will quote another part of this document to you which says, I quote: "The results of work of the Crisis Staff were evident as soon as its first activities started. The people who originated from Kravica were willing and ready to help their village including the sending of volunteers to defend it. Soldiers who arrived, volunteers who left their jobs in Belgrade and other places in order to take weapons and defend Kravica confirmed there. Goran Nikolic was one the first volunteers to arrive from Belgrade, then Milan Milosevic, also known as Minja, came and organised a village defence of the following line, Banjevici, Ocenovici and Begici. He brought about 20 men who were originally from Ocenovici and Banjevici with him from Belgrade." Did you know that in the area of Jezestica and Kravica it was not only local Serbs who were fighting but also volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know this?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned at the beginning that I had my own Motorola which I had brought with me as a police officer, and I listened in to their conversations on the Motorola, and they would also often shout to each other. The terrain was such that they would shout and they would often yell threats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you clarify to Their Honours how you came by the power needed to use the Motorola?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the gentlemen were not believe me, but I had an improvised device. I used something called a Cekrk, using a mini motor from a cement mixer, or I would use the motor from my windscreen wiper, and two or one man would turn this by hand, and that was the power source.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Cekrk is a winch, the interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was a mechanical way of producing energy. Thank you, Your Honours. I understand that we were sitting until a quarter past 6.00 today, so this is a convenient place to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you very much for your cooperation, Ms. Vidovic. We will adjourn for today. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15 in this same courtroom. How could you doing time-wise? I would like to see this gentleman go back home end of business on Friday, if possible. All right. So good evening to everyone, and we'll meet again tomorrow. And one moment before we leave. Mr. Ademovic, between today and tomorrow and then subsequently between each day until you finish your testimony, you're not to communicate with anyone and discuss with anyone or mention or let anyone mention to you or discuss with you the substance of the events that you are testifying upon. I'm sure that as an ex-policeman you understand exactly what I mean. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
